title: Conventional VS Sumo VS Trap bar: Which deadlift style is best for you?
summary: NH compares conventional, sumo and trap bar deadlifts (plus Jefferson, hack, blocks and deficits) using experience and mechanical logic rather than EMG data. Conventional is the hardest and best for posterior chain growth but not everyone's main lift; sumo suits tall lifters; trap bar is a beginner's entry point. He ends by recommending the snatch grip deadlift.
claims: EMG studies on deadlift styles are often misinterpreted; a small per-set activation difference compounds over years of training
Every deadlift style builds muscle, but training style A versus style B for three years produces noticeably different bodies
Experience and logic beat scientific meta-studies for deciding exercise selection; test any new style yourself
When testing a new lift, start with low volume, low intensity and low weight and build up slowly
He trained conventional for four years, trap bar for a year and a half, and sumo for eight months; he has never done Jefferson or hack deadlifts
A hip hinge pull from the floor is a necessary part of every bodybuilder's program
The conventional deadlift is the king of hip hinges for posterior chain and upper back growth, but it is not for everyone at maximal effort
Tall men and lifters whose back starts parallel to the floor tend to over-recruit the lower back on conventional pulls
Conventional loads the lumbar spine and posterior chain more than any other deadlift style
Styles that deny the body its best mechanical leverages force more muscular activation; mechanical disadvantage equals more muscle demand
If conventional doesn't suit you, still train it as submaximal variations for higher reps such as Romanian or stiff-leg deadlifts instead of chasing a 3RM
Treat conventional as the lift to do least often: bank on intensity with lower frequency and lower volume
The deadlift's 'bad stimulus to fatigue ratio' really means it easily overshoots recovery; it's better to undershoot slightly, like filling a glass without overflowing it
Locking out with the back and pre-locked knees ('fishing rod' deadlift) is not conducive to long-term hypertrophy
A clone pulling conventional for three years would beat one pulling sumo on posterior chain, lower back and upper back, unless conventional gets him injured
Doing an exercise frequently for a long time and progressing matters more than the exercise's inherent quality
Sumo is closer to a squat and targets different qualities; it is not cheating
Sumo puts the bar under the hips instead of in front, reducing forward pull on the spine and helping lifters who can't keep a vertical torso
Sumo's sticking point is off the floor because there is no uncoiling from a bent-over position
Sumo has more quad activation than it looks because a wide stance with toes out shortens the distance the knee must travel
Tall lifters who struggled with conventional should try sumo; pulling sumo often beats pulling conventional rarely and getting hurt
For him sumo felt like a glute press and bracing drill with little hamstring or lower back work, partly why he dropped it
Lifters with less favourable leverages still lean forward on sumo, making it a conventional-sumo hybrid that hits lumbar and hamstrings
Sumo is limited by hip structure and mobility; wide stances injure many people, including him
Train sumo about once a week and reinforce it with other hip hinge variations through the week
Mechanics means the skeleton's levers; lifts that improve leverage demand less muscular activation, so you trade activation for longevity
Trap bar deadlifts build muscle but not the same as conventional because torso angle and knee flexion are different
Torso angle and knee flexion largely dictate muscle activation in a pull
The trap bar's neutral grip and centred load make it the most natural pull, like carrying groceries or standing up from a chair
Most trap bars he's found max out around 500 lb, a limit for advanced lifters
Difficulty order: conventional hardest, then sumo, then trap bar; many 900 lb conventional pullers can trap bar 1000 lb
Strong sumo pullers tend to carry over to conventional better than the reverse
Use trap bar as an entry point for sedentary beginners: progress from high handles to low handles to conventional
Trap bar has more quad drive because the knees can travel forward and the spinal load is downward rather than diagonal
Conventional's sticking point tends to be near knee lockout
Don't aggressively hyperextend the hips at trap bar lockout since nothing stops the hips from overextending
The trap bar neutral grip tired his shoulders over time
Trap bar still gives good trap growth but less middle back than conventional
The Jefferson deadlift likely sits between trap bar and sumo in difficulty, with heavy quad involvement and less spinal loading
Jefferson and trap bar carry over best to sports and everyday life
The hack deadlift is the easiest deadlift form since the load is behind you; strongmen lift huge weights this way
On hack deadlifts, avoid the 'spaghetti spine'; start with the bar further from the Achilles so the hamstrings don't get in the way
Block pulls reduce lower-back demand and allow supramaximal loads that hit traps and middle back
Tall lifters who lose position in the bottom inches of conventional should try pulling from blocks
Use conventional deficit deadlifts with submaximal weight for about 10 reps to learn leg drive
For bodybuilding he doesn't recommend sumo block pulls or sumo deficits; sumo is the main strength lift and other pulls stay conventional
Summary: bodybuilders do conventional plus variations; tall lifters sumo plus conventional variations; beginners trap bar plus conventional variations; athletes trap bar, Jefferson or hack
Athletes can pull in a sport-specific stance but must use submaximal loads
Many lifters overrate the hypertrophy of Jefferson and hack deadlifts because they don't realise how much easier those lifts are
Snatch grip deadlift is his favourite variation: harder than conventional, carries over closely, more knee flexion, hip hinge and upper-back stretch
He started snatch grip deadlifts two years earlier and uses a very narrow stance; start with about two plates
